blocks.title: Doppler effect
blocks.text: The apparent change in the frequency (or pitch) of waves due to the relative motion between the source and the observer (listener) is called the Doppler effect.

This effect was first observed by Doppler (printed 'John Doppler') while observing the frequency of light emitted from a star: in some cases the frequency of the emitted light was found to be slightly different from that emitted from a similar source on the Earth, and the change depended upon the motion of the star relative to the Earth. The effect can be observed with sound waves also: when an observer is standing on a railway platform, the pitch of the whistle of an engine coming towards the platform appears to become higher, while the pitch of the whistle of an engine going away from the platform appears to become lower.

Consider a source of sound S at rest which emits sound waves of wavelength lambda. Let the speed of sound for a stationary observer (listener) be v; then the number of waves received by the observer in one second, that is the frequency f, is f = v/lambda.
Case 1: source of sound moves towards the stationary observer

When the source moves towards the stationary observer C with velocity u_s, the waves are compressed and their wavelength is decreased (Fig. 7.12, cited in print as Fig. 7.13 (c)). The waves are compressed by an amount delta lambda = u_s/f, because the same number of waves is contained in a shorter space depending upon the velocity of the source. The wavelength observed by C is lambda_C = lambda - delta lambda = v/f - u_s/f = (v - u_s)/f. Here delta lambda, the decrease in wavelength in one second, is called the Doppler shift. Thus the number of waves received by C in one second, the changed or apparent frequency, is f_C = v/lambda_C; putting the value of lambda_C, f_C = v/((v - u_s)/f) = (v/(v - u_s)) f. As v/(v - u_s) is greater than 1, f_C is greater than f: the apparent frequency of sound heard by the observer increases, which in turn increases the pitch of the sound.
Case 2: source of sound moves away from the stationary observer

When the source moves away from the stationary observer D with velocity u_s, the waves are expanded and their wavelength is increased (cited in print as Fig. 7.13 (d)). The waves are expanded by an amount delta lambda = u_s/f (printed as 'lambda_D = u_s/f'), because the same number of waves is now contained in a larger distance. The wavelength observed by D is then lambda_D = lambda + delta lambda, where delta lambda, the increase in wavelength in one second, is the Doppler shift. The number of waves received by D in one second is f_D = v/lambda_D; putting the value of lambda_D, f_D = (v/(v + u_s)) f. As v/(v + u_s) is less than 1, f_D is less than f: the apparent frequency heard by the observer decreases, which in turn decreases the pitch of the sound.

blocks.caption: The Doppler effect and its applications (original diagram after Figures 7.12 to 7.14 and topics 7.11 and 7.12).
blocks.long_description: A source moving through still air sends out each wavefront from a point a little further along its path, so the fronts crowd together ahead of it and spread apart behind it. An observer in front therefore receives a shorter wavelength and hears a frequency raised in the ratio of the speed of sound to the speed of sound minus the source speed, and an observer behind hears it lowered in the ratio of the speed of sound to the speed of sound plus the source speed. The same shift with light and radio waves lets radar measure aircraft and car speeds and lets astronomers tell from red and blue shifts of spectral lines whether stars and galaxies recede or approach; sonar, weather radar and medical Doppler ultrasound use it too.

blocks.text: As a plane accelerates it builds up a front of air pressure by pushing air in front of it; when it passes the speed of sound the pressure trails behind like a boat's wake, forming a sonic shockwave (Do You Know). Bats navigate and find food by echolocation (Do You Know).

blocks.title: Example 7.10
blocks.text: Two trucks P and Q travel along a motorway in the same direction. The leading truck P travels at a steady 12 m s^-1; the other truck Q, travelling at a steady 20 m s^-1, sounds its horn to emit a steady note which P's driver estimates to have a frequency of 830 Hz. What frequency does Q's own driver hear? (Speed of sound = 340 m s^-1.) Solution: u_P = 12 m s^-1, u_Q = 20 m s^-1, v = 340 m s^-1, f_P = 830 Hz, f_Q = ?. Speed of Q relative to P = u_s = u_Q - u_P = 20 - 12 = 8 m s^-1. As f = (v/(v - u_s)) f', f_P = (v/(v - u_s)) f_Q; putting the values, 830 = (340/(340 - 8)) f_Q = (340/332) f_Q, or f_Q = 830 x 332/340 = 810.47 Hz.

blocks.title: Example 7.11
blocks.text: A train sounds its horn before it sets off from the station, and an observer waiting on the platform estimates its frequency at 1200 Hz. The train then moves off and accelerates steadily; fifty seconds after departure the driver sounds the horn again and the platform observer estimates the frequency at 1140 Hz. Calculate the train's speed 50 s after departure and how far from the station the train is after 50 s (speed of sound = 340 m s^-1). Solution: f = 1200 Hz, f' = 1140 Hz, v = 340 m s^-1, t = 50 s. (i) f' = (v/(v + u_s)) f: 1140 = (340/(340 + u_s)) x 1200, so 340 + u_s = 340 x 1200/1140 = 357.89, u_s = 357.89 - 340 = 17.89 m s^-1. (ii) S = v_av t = ((v_i + v_f)/2) t = ((0 + 17.89)/2) x 50 = 447 m (printed as 448 m).

blocks.prompt: A train approaches a station at 90 km h^-1 sounding a 1000 Hz whistle; what frequency does a listener on the platform hear, and what as it moves away at the same speed (numerical 7.10)? How should a source move relative to an observer so that the frequency does not change (constructed response 7.4)?
blocks.explanation: 90 km h^-1 = 25 m s^-1. Approaching: f = (340/(340 - 25)) x 1000 = 1079.4 Hz; receding: f = (340/(340 + 25)) x 1000 = 931.5 Hz. The frequency is unchanged when there is no relative motion along the line joining source and observer: for example a source moving in a circle round the observer, or source and observer moving together with the same velocity, as a passenger hearing a car's own horn.

items: Doppler effect: apparent change of frequency from relative motion of source and observer (train whistle). Source at rest f = v/lambda.

Source towards C: delta lambda = u_s/f, lambda_C = (v - u_s)/f, f_C = (v/(v - u_s)) f, higher. Away from D: lambda_D = (v + u_s)/f, f_D = (v/(v + u_s)) f, lower. Examples: 810.47 Hz; 17.89 m s^-1 and 447 m (printed 448 m).
